info.bio:
Geethali Norah Jones Shankar (30 de marzo de 1979), conocida como Norah Jones, es una cantante y pianista estadounidense de jazz y música pop.

Su voz cálida e íntima, su sencillez y un enorme talento ha enamorado a medio mundo y con su primer disco “Come Away With me” ha conseguido vender más de 20 millones de copias y 8 premios Grammy y hasta la fecha la cantante lleva más de 39 millones de copias vendidas en todo el mundo. Su música combina elementos de jazz, soul y country.

En 2007 hace su primera aparación en el cine en "My Blueberry Nights", a manos de Wong Kar-Wai.

El 30 de marzo de 1979, meses después de terminarse la relación entre el maestro indio del sitar, Ravi Shankar, y la enfermera Sue Jones, nació la pequeña Norah.

Norah y su madre vivieron en Nueva York hasta que la niña cumplió cuatro años. Entonces se mudaron a Grapevine (cerca de Dallas, Texas), donde vivió hasta los veinte. En su casa nunca faltaron discos de los clásicos del blues y del jazz: Billie Holiday, Etta James, Aretha Franklin, Ray Charles, Bill Evans, Joni Mitchell... A la influencia musical materna hay que sumar la que recibió de su abuela, una apasionada del recio country de los outlaws, desde Hank Williams a Willie Nelson.

Norah empezó a estudiar canto y se sumó al coro de la iglesia para cantar gospel, al tiempo que iniciaba las clases de piano y saxofón (a los siete). Estaba lejos de ser una alumna modelo: era bastante vaga y dejó el estudio varias veces. Sin el esfuerzo de su madre, su abuela, y sus profesores Renetta Frisque y Julie Bonk, probablemente hubiese abandonado el camino musical.

Cuando creció se matriculó en una escuela de artes y nunca faltaba en las actuaciones para cumpleaños y concursos musicales. Su primer contacto con el jazz lo tuvo en Dallas, al ingresar en su adolescencia en el Instituto Broker T. Washirable. En 1996 y 1997 ganó varios premios de interpretación y composición para estudiantes. Al finalizar el instituto entró en la Universidad de North Texas, donde estudió piano y teoría en el programa de jazz. Allí se especializó en teclado de jazz y formó su primer grupo. De ahí pasó a tocar el piano y cantar regularmente en un restaurante italiano.

Con veinte años cumplidos, Norah volvió a Nueva York para unas breves vacaciones y ya no quiso volver a Texas, para disgusto de su madre. Poco antes había tomado contacto con un grupo de músicos de aquella ciudad y quedó prendada. Una vez en “La gran manzana”, pronto hizo pie en el fértil circuito de garitos de conciertos de Greenwich Village y colaboró con diversas bandas. Durante dos años se ganó la vida cantando en salones de jazz, almuerzos y happy hours, muchas veces ante menos de quince personas y cobrando sólo de las propinas que les daban los parroquianos. Sin embargo, en esa época supo que quería vivir de cantar en vivo y que iba a hacer todo lo posible por lograrlo. Abandonó la universidad, empezó a escribir sus propias canciones, formó parte del combo de funk fusion, Wax Poetic, y finalmente montó su propio grupo con el bajista Lee Alexander, el guitarrista y compositor de Don’t Know Why, Jesse Harris, y el baterista Dan Rieser. Por esa época se estabilizó como cantante en el club nocturno The Living Room

En uno de esos conciertos la escuchó Shell White, miembro de la discográfica EMI, una noche del año 2000. Le gustó lo que oía y le pidió un demo con sus canciones. Éste se lo llevó a su amigo Bruce Lundvall, director de Blue Note, el reputado sello de jazz. Y acertó, porque esa compañía estaba en la búsqueda de nuevos artistas.

La propuesta de Norah no podía ser más tentadora: una voz joven y sugerente, plena de cálida sensualidad, cantando casi como si desvelara algún íntimo secreto. Lundvall la contrató con haber escuchado apenas tres canciones de ese cassette y le encargó al productor Craig Street que trabajara el material de Norah y la rodeara con instrumentistas de lujo. El resultado, mucho más pop que la versión final, no convenció a nadie y Lundvall le encargó a su productor estrella, Arif Mardin, una nueva versión, que se concentrara en la voz. El paquete estaba listo y Come Away With Me, su debut discográfico, salió a la venta en febrero de 2002, sin campañas masivas, ni un hit agresivo sonando en todas las radios. Sin embargo, el boca a boca hizo su trabajo y el disco se empezó a vender cada vez más. Para el otoño ya había sobrepasado el millón de copias vendidas y todos estaban maravillados. También se convirtió en platino en Holanda, Australia, Portugal y Hong Kong; doble platino en Gran Bretaña, Irlanda y Singapur; y quíntuple platino en Nueva Zelanda. El total de ventas alrededor del mundo sobrepasa los 18 millones de copias. Además, fue la gran triunfadora de la 45 edición de los Grammy entregados en 2003, con sus ocho estatuillas ganadas, incluidas mejor álbum, canción, disco del año y mejor artista novel, siendo la gran sorpresa de la noche ya que prácticamente le arrebató 3 estatuillas de la mano a Eminem, incluido el de disco del año, ya que según las apuestas favorecían a Eminem.

Dos años después de la publicación de su álbum de debut, "Come Away with Me", Norah Jones regresa con "Feels Like Home".La cantante-pianista-compositora vuelve a hacer equipo con el productor Arif Mardin, el ingeniero de sonido Jay Newland y su grupo habitual en directo. Nos ofrece un conjunto de canciones compuestas por ella, los miembros de su grupo y por el cantante y compositor Richard Julian. Jones también hace versiones de varias canciones incluyendo "Be Here To Love Me" de Townes Van Zandt y "Melancholia" de Duke Ellington, canción para la que ella escribió las letras y la re-tituló con el nombre de "Don’t Miss You At All".

En 2007, saca su tercer álbum de estudio, Not Too Late.

info.wikipedia:
Geethali Norah Shankar Jones (Nueva York, 30 de marzo de 1979), conocida como Norah Jones, es una cantante, compositora, pianista, actriz y multinstrumentista estadounidense. Ganadora de nueve premios Grammy, ha vendido más de 60 millones de discos y sencillos. Su música combina elementos de jazz, blues, soul, country y pop. [1]​

Protagonizó la película My Blueberry Nights y ha realizado dos cameos, el primero en la película Amor a segunda vista (2002) y en Ted (2012).[2]​

Norah Jones nació en Bedford-Stuyvesant, hija biológica del fallecido y famoso sitarista indio Ravi Shankar y de la productora de conciertos Sue Jones. Hermana, por parte paterna, de la también sitarista Anoushka Shankar.

Junto con su madre, ella vivió en Nueva York hasta que cumplió cuatro años. Entonces, se mudaron a Grapevine (cerca de Dallas, Texas), donde estuvo hasta los veinte. De esta época data su primer interés por la música, que se materializaba en la audición de discos de clásicos del blues y del jazz como Billie Holiday, Etta James, Aretha Franklin, Ray Charles, Bill Evans, Joni Mitchell y otros. A estas influencias, hay que añadir las recibidas por vía de su abuela, aficionada al country de los outlaws, desde Hank Williams a Willie Nelson.

Norah empezó a estudiar canto y se sumó al coro de la iglesia para cantar gospel, al tiempo que iniciaba las clases de piano y saxofón (a los siete).

Cuando creció, se matriculó en una escuela de artes. Su primer contacto con el jazz lo tuvo en Dallas, al ingresar en su adolescencia en el Booker T. Washington High School for the Performing and Visual Arts (Secundario de artes escénicas y visuales). En 1996 y 1997 ganó varios premios de composición e interpretación para estudiantes. Al finalizar el instituto, entró en la Universidad de North Texas, donde estudió piano y teoría en el programa de jazz. Allí se especializó en teclado de jazz y formó su primer grupo. Durante dos años se ganó la vida cantando en salones de jazz, almuerzos y happy hours, muchas veces ante menos de quince personas y cobrando sólo de las propinas que les daban los parroquianos.

Abandonó la universidad, empezó a escribir sus propias canciones, formó parte del combo de funk fusion, Wax Poetic y, finalmente, montó su propio grupo con el bajista Lee Alexander, el guitarrista y compositor de «Don’t Know Why», Jesse Harris, y el baterista Dan Rieser. Por esa época, se estabilizó como cantante en el club nocturno The Living Room.

En uno de esos conciertos la escuchó Shell White, miembro de la discográfica EMI, una noche del año 2000. Le gustó lo que oía y le pidió un demo con sus canciones. Este se lo llevó a su amigo Bruce Lundvall, director de Blue Note, el reputado sello de jazz. Y acertó, porque esa compañía estaba en la búsqueda de nuevos artistas.

Lundvall la contrató con haber escuchado apenas tres canciones de ese casete y le encargó al productor Craig Street que trabajara el material de Norah y la rodeara con instrumentistas de lujo. El resultado, mucho más pop que la versión final, no convenció a nadie y Lundvall le encargó a su productor estrella, Arif Mardin, una nueva versión, que se concentrara en la voz. El paquete estaba listo y Come Away With Me, su debut discográfico, salió a la venta en febrero de 2002, sin campañas masivas, ni un hit agresivo sonando en todas las radios. Sin embargo, el boca a boca hizo su trabajo y el disco se empezó a vender cada vez más. Para el otoño ya había sobrepasado el millón de copias vendidas y todos estaban maravillados. También se convirtió en platino en Holanda, Australia, Portugal y Hong Kong; doble platino en Gran Bretaña, Irlanda y Singapur; y quíntuple platino en Nueva Zelanda. El total de ventas alrededor del mundo sobrepasa los 18 millones de copias. Además, fue la gran triunfadora de la 45 edición de los Grammy entregados en 2003, con sus cinco estatuillas ganadas, incluidas mejor álbum, canción, disco del año y mejor artista novel, siendo la gran sorpresa de la noche ya que prácticamente le arrebató 3 estatuillas de la mano a Eminem, incluido el de disco del año, aunque las apuestas favorecían a Eminem.

Dos años después de la publicación de su álbum de debut, "Come Away with Me", Norah Jones regresa con "Feels Like Home". La cantante-pianista-compositora vuelve a hacer equipo con el productor Arif Mardin, el ingeniero de sonido Jay Newland y su grupo habitual en directo. Nos ofrece un conjunto de canciones compuestas por ella, los miembros de su grupo y por el cantante y compositor Richard Julian. Jones también hace versiones de varias canciones incluyendo "Be Here To Love Me" de Townes Van Zandt y "Melancholia" de Duke Ellington, canción para la que ella escribió las letras y la re-tituló con el nombre de "Don’t Miss You At All".

En 2007, saca su tercer álbum de estudio, Not Too Late, y lanza 5 sencillos. El álbum vende alrededor de 7 millones de copias.

El 17 de noviembre de 2009 salió a la venta su cuarta producción titulada The Fall, la cual contiene trece temas, además de seis temas en la versión de lujo. El disco incluye las colaboraciones de Marc Ribot, James Gadson, Joey Waronker o James Poyser, entre otros.

En 2010, salió a la venta su quinta producción titulada ...Featuring, en el cual Norah Jones canta con 18 artistas, entre los que están Foo Fighters, Belle and Sebastian, Dolly Parton, y muchos más.

En 2012 sale su sexto material inédito con el nombre de Little Broken Hearts, y su primer sencillo fue "Happy Pills".
El 25 de noviembre de 2013 fue lanzado Foreverly, es un álbum colaborativo del guitarrista de Green Day Billie Joe Armstrong y la cantante y compositora de jazz / pop Norah Jones.

El sexto álbum de estudio en solitario de Norah Jones, fue lanzado el 7 de octubre de 2016 a través de Blue Note Records. El álbum cuenta con nueve canciones originales y tres versiones.

Begin Again es el séptimo álbum de estudio de Norah Jones, lanzado a través de Blue Note Records el 12 de abril de 2019. El álbum también se llamó "compilación de sencillos", que Jones grabó desde 2018 hasta 2019, e incluye colaboraciones con Jeff Tweedy y Thomas Bartlett.

The Little Willies es una banda formada el 2003, con Norah Jones en las voces y el piano, Richard Julian en las voces, Jim Campilongo en la guitarra, Lee Alexander en el bajo y Dan Rieser en la percusión. Hasta el momento han sacado dos discos, The Little Willies (2006), y For The Good Times (2012)

Peeping Tom es un álbum colaborativo de Mike Patton, lanzado el 2006. Jones apareció en la canción número 10, "Sucker".

El 12 de mayo de 2006, Norah Jones (disfrazada con una peluca rubia, mucho maquillaje, mallas y pantalones muy cortos) apareció en una banda llamada "El Madmo" como teloneros de Pela. Consistía de "El" (Daru Oda de Handsome Band) "Maddie" (Norah Jones) y "Mo" (Andrew Borger).
El 20 de mayo de 2008 salió a la venta su primer disco, que lleva el nombre de la banda.
El Tracklist es:

1. Carlo!
2. Head in a Vise
3. Vampire Guy
4. GGW
5. Sweet Adrenaline
6. Attack of the Rock People
7. The Best Part
8. Fantasy Guy
9. I Like it Low
10. Scary Lady
11. Nonny Goat Mon
12. Rock Yer Balls Off

Colaboró en la canción "Virginia Moon" del álbum "In Your Honor" lanzado en el año 2005.

Colaboró en la canción "Little Lou, Ugly Jack, Prophet John" del álbum "Belle and Sebastian Write About Love" lanzado en el año 2010.

En 2007, Norah Jones aparece como parte del álbum "River: The Joni Letters", de Herbie Hancock como un tributo a Joni Mitchell. Norah canta la pista "Court and Spark".

Pone voz en el disco de la banda titulado "New York City".

En 2020 compone dos canciones colaborativas con el cantautor brasileño Rodrigo Amarante llamadas "Falling" y "I forgot".

En 2023, Jones apareció en el sencillo "Paradise II" del octavo álbum de estudio del rapero Logic, College Park .

En 2023, Jones colaboró con la música de jazz islandesa Laufey en dos temas, grabando una versión de la clásica canción navideña "Have Yourself A Merry Little Christmas" y lanzando una canción original titulada "Better Than Snow".

scenes.name: Voces del jazz moderno: Ella, Sarah, Carmen y el vocalese
scenes.author: Ted Gioia
scenes.desc: La faceta más ligada a la tradición del jazz de los setenta y ochenta. Norman Granz convierte a Ella Fitzgerald, ya superventas desde la banda de Chick Webb, en una artista mayor con los songbooks dedicados a Porter, Gershwin, Arlen, Ellington y Berlin y los directos de Berlín y Roma; en Pablo la empareja con Basie o Joe Pass. Carmen McRae y Betty Carter prolongan a Billie Holiday con libertades rítmicas casi vanguardistas; Sheila Jordan y Mel Tormé siguen sus propios caminos. El vocalese de Eddie Jefferson y Jon Hendricks pone letra a solos famosos y convierte al cantante en un griot que narra la historia del jazz (Joni Mitchell con «Goodbye Pork Pie Hat», Manhattan Transfer). Bobby McFerrin, imitador de metales y director de orquesta, triunfa con «Don't Worry, Be Happy» y se niega a explotar el éxito.

podcast.title: Contribution to Herbie Hancock's Album (2007)
podcast.body: Nora Jones also sang on Herbie Hancock's 2008 Album of the Year winner, "River: The Joni Letters," a CD of jazz covers of Joni Mitchell's songs. "Nora Jones sang on Hancock's album too."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: And the Grammy Goes to… Edition Part 2

podcast.title: Artistic Evolution and Avoiding Pigeonholing
podcast.body: Nora Jones expressed excitement about continuously "finding stuff" and getting "into songwriting" after her debut album, where she only wrote a few songs. She was eager to avoid being "pigeonholed" into a specific sound like a piano trio and deliberately explored new genres, such as bluegrass, which influenced her second album to be "a little more country." Don Was compared her artistic evolution to Miles Davis, noting how she, like Miles, always sounded like herself but kept it interesting by "changing the textures." "Did the success of come away with me? Were you trying to avoid getting pigeonholed into piano, trio? I was just excited to keep finding stuff."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Introducing Broken Record - Norah Jones Begins Again

podcast.title: Blue Note Record Deal Negotiation
podcast.body: Nora Jones secured a meeting with Bruce Lentval, the head of Blue Note Records, after an EMI publishing contact heard her play at her 21st birthday jazz brunch gig at The Garage on 7th Avenue. She brought a three-song demo for the meeting. When Lentval asked if she wanted to be a jazz or pop singer, she confidently responded "jazz singer," which she described as the "correct answer" for Blue Note. Her primary aspirations at the time were simply to pay rent and transition from restaurant gigs to club performances, rather than securing a record deal. "Did you aspire to get a record, you know? I was aspiring to pay my rent and to get a gig at a non-brunch venue."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Introducing Broken Record - Norah Jones Begins Again

podcast.title: Bruce Lentval's Candid Feedback
podcast.body: Years after her early releases, Bruce Lentval, then head of Blue Note Records, candidly admitted to Nora Jones that he initially disliked her albums "The Fall" and "Little Broken Hearts" (with the injured mass). He told her, "I'm going to be honest with you. I didn't like those records when you turned them in. They're not really my thing, but I think now I like them and I get it. Now I get it." Nora appreciated his honesty, noting he "never kissed my butt." "He never kissed my butt. He never told me he liked them. So I never really thought about him not saying anything but like it was fine."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Introducing Broken Record - Norah Jones Begins Again

podcast.title: Childhood Music Tastes
podcast.body: As a child, Nora Jones was a fan of pop music from the American Top 40, enjoying artists like Paul Abdul (whose album she considered a "great record" with "really good songs"), Milli Vanilli, and Bobby Brown. Her earliest musical purchases included Digital Underground's "The Humpty Dance" as her first record and MC Hammer as her first concert experience. She fondly recalled listening to K-Earth 101 every weekend. "I loved Paul Abdul. That album, that one album was just, it was huge when I was little."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Introducing Broken Record - Norah Jones Begins Again

podcast.title: Childhood Personality and Self-Awareness
podcast.body: Nora Jones described herself as a generally shy child, particularly after seventh grade. In sixth grade, she felt "completely unaware of how I was perceived" and "completely open," but an encounter with "mean girls" in school led her to become more self-aware and self-conscious, causing her to "kind of went inside." "I was kind of shy. I wasn't that shy until seventh grade."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Introducing Broken Record - Norah Jones Begins Again

podcast.title: Collaborative Recording Pace
podcast.body: The recording of Norah Jones' new album with Leon Michels involved short, frequent sessions (11 AM to 2 PM), pieced together whenever possible due to their children's school schedules. This contrasted with her previous album made with "the Angel Mouse," which involved two months in the studio. Norah found this new, flexible approach "so fun." "This was just here and there and dribs and drabs and always short days because our kids were in school and just 11 to 2 and all right, cool."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: College Experience and Dropout
podcast.body: Nora Jones attended the University of North Texas, known for its strong jazz program, for two years. She initially focused on piano but later joined the vocal ensemble for jazz singers, though singing was not her main academic focus. She dropped out after failing her classical piano jury, primarily because she hadn't practiced, realizing she didn't need a music degree for her career aspirations and was busy playing in two bands and doing gigs. "I ended up going to North Texas. Yeah. And two years from now."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Daughter of Ravi Shankar
podcast.body: Nora Jones is the daughter of Ravi Shankar, who was famously known as The Beatles' favorite sitar player. "Nora Jones is the daughter of Ravai Shankar, the Beatles favorite Cittar player."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: More Musical Offspring

podcast.title: Discovery of "Heart Ake"
podcast.body: Norah Jones discovered the song "Heart Ake" by Lowell George around the time she was making her second record. Kevin Bright, who played guitar on her first album, introduced her to Lowell George's work, specifically the album "Thanks, I'll Eat It Here." She subsequently found and admired a bootleg demo of "Heart Ake" featuring Lowell George and Linda Ronstadt. "I discovered it maybe probably around this time I was making my second record I think Kevin Bright, who played on my guitar my first record, turned me on to Lowell George."

podcast.title: Duet with Andre 3000
podcast.body: Grammy Queen Nora Jones, who had won Album of the Year herself just two years prior, featured in a duet with Andre 3000 on Outcast's *Speaker Box, Slash, The Love Below* album, contributing to its diverse musical breadth. "The album even featured a duet between Andre and Grammy Queen Nora Jones, who had taken album of the year herself just two years earlier."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Shake It Like a Polaroid Picture Edition Part 2

podcast.title: Early Gigs and Songwriting Inspiration in NYC
podcast.body: After moving to New York City and dropping out of college, Nora took restaurant gigs, which paid less than her previous job in Texas. She immersed herself in the city's vibrant music scene, regularly attending clubs like Smalls and Tonic (an avant-garde venue), hearing diverse genres from Brazilian bands to jazz. She was inspired by songwriter friends performing at The Living Room, which prompted her to start writing songs again after a long hiatus since a high school synthesizer class. Her mother sent her an old guitar, on which she learned simple chords and wrote her breakthrough song, "Come Away With Me." "I was just, I was going to Smalls every night and watching people play and just so in love with going to hear music every night."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Introducing Broken Record - Norah Jones Begins Again

podcast.title: Early Musical Upbringing and Exploration
podcast.body: Nora Jones grew up in Grapevine, Texas, a suburb of Dallas that was small during her childhood but later became a highly developed area. She moved frequently and attended various schools, including a six-month period living in Alaska. She played saxophone in marching band in ninth grade, eventually quitting piano lessons but later reconnecting with music through a saxophone teacher (John Rosina) and a jazz piano teacher (Julie Bonk), which introduced her to the jazz scene in Denton, Texas. She also gained early singing experience in the church choir at Grapevine Methodist Church. "I kind of bounced around though and I bounced around schools a lot and we moved to Alaska for six months."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Introducing Broken Record - Norah Jones Begins Again

podcast.title: Evolving Piano Technique
podcast.body: Norah Jones has evolved her piano playing, now utilizing the full range of the instrument, exploring "way low or way high," which she notes she never used to do. "Yeah sometimes and sometimes like I'll use the whole piano, which I never used to do. I wouldn't think to go way low or way high."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Introducing Broken Record - Norah Jones Begins Again

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Introducing Broken Record - Norah Jones Begins Again

podcast.title: Family Relationships and Media Scrutiny
podcast.body: Her fame brought complicated dynamics to her family relationships, specifically with her father, Ravi Shankar, with whom she had reunited at age 18, and her half-sister, Anoushka Shankar. Media representations of her family were often "never quite right," causing distress to her mother or father. "So someone in within your family? Yeah, like either my mom felt like it wasn't represented right or my dad did or you know like it was just kind of that was actually a really hard thing for me to be honest."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Favorite Piano Player - Aretha Franklin
podcast.body: Norah Jones considers Aretha Franklin one of her favorite piano players, admiring her "feel." She notes that she loved Aretha's piano playing on recordings even before she knew it was Aretha herself playing. "She's always been my favorite One of the best feels out there."

podcast.title: First Public Performance in NYC and Audience Connection
podcast.body: Nora Jones' first public performance in a dedicated listening venue like The Living Room was a significant moment. Performing with Jesse Harris and her bassist Lee Alexander, she experienced a profound connection with the audience: "you could hear a pen drop. Nobody was talking. Everybody was listening." This attentive reception, coupled with passing a tip jar, contrasted sharply with her previous restaurant gigs where nobody listened. "it was the first time I'd played in a place like that. And they passed a tip jar around and you couldn't. You could hear a pen drop. Nobody was talking. Everybody was listening."

podcast.title: Friendship with Older Producers
podcast.body: Norah Jones developed deep friendships with producers Arif Mardin and Bruce Lundvall, often going to lunch, drinking martinis for hours, and discussing personal relationships, which she found humorous given their age difference. "I could go to lunch with Arif or Bruce and we could drink martinis for hours and just blah, blah, blah, blah. Talk about relationships. Like I would talk about my boyfriend. You know what I mean? They were like my friends."

podcast.title: High School Performing Arts Experience
podcast.body: Nora attended a performing arts high school in Dallas, which she described as a great institution for "people of artistic interest." While her major was jazz piano, she also took classical piano (at which she admitted being "horrible") and a synthesis ensemble class where she learned on instruments like the DX7 and Moog. The teacher encouraged songwriting, and she even contributed a song to a cassette tape, though she disliked it due to the synth strings. Notable alumni of the school include Roy Hargrove and Erykah Badu. "I went to performing arts high school in Dallas, which was completely all people of artistic interest."

podcast.title: Initial Hesitation with Arif Mardin
podcast.body: Norah Jones was initially confused and hesitant about producer Arif Mardin joining her project, fearing he would impose unwanted strings or change her sound, despite his legendary status and her admiration for his work with Donnie Hathaway. "I was a little confused. I was like, well, you like the demos we did on our own. Should we just do that?"

podcast.title: Inspiration from Sleeping/Dreaming State
podcast.body: For her new album, Norah Jones found many ideas came to her in the transitional state between dreaming and sleeping. She would wake up and quietly record these thoughts as voice memos, a process she notes became more prevalent during the pandemic. "That moment right when you're falling asleep, I had all these ideas and I would just get up and do a little quiet. Try not to wake up my husband or go to the bathroom and do quiet little voice memo of it."

podcast.title: Mimicking and Finding Her Authentic Voice
podcast.body: Growing up, Nora Jones learned by mimicking her favorite singers, including Aretha Franklin (especially harmonies for "A Natural Woman") and Billie Holiday (whom she portrayed in a high school program, singing "Strange Fruit" and actively trying to emulate her sound). She was also "obsessed with Saravan" (Sarah Vaughan). A college friend's observation of her "Texas twang" in a jazz standard made her realize she could "kind of be myself" and didn't "have to imitate Ella... or Saravan." She values "imperfect or weird" voices that "embody themselves." "I tried to mimic Aritha and all her, all her background singing, you know, I was always doing the harmonies to Aena Wave."

podcast.title: Mixed Race Background and Identity
podcast.body: Nora Jones' mother is white and her father is black, making her mixed race. She stated she did not experience racism but frequently encountered "nosiness" from people asking "What are you?". In Texas, she was often assumed to be Mexican and addressed in Spanish, which she couldn't speak, leading to awkward moments. In high school, some thought she was half black, and people "just didn't know what to make of me." "I'm mixed as well. I'm black and white. My mom's white, my dad's black."

podcast.title: Pianist Skills and Live Performance Preference
podcast.body: Don Was praised Nora Jones as an "incredible pianist" with "incredibly sophisticated" voicings and a deep understanding of theory, scales, and modes, though she admits to not having a lot of "chops" or playing very fast. She feels she has gotten "a lot better in the last 10 years" due to playing more piano live, often in a trio format. She finds it challenging to sing without accompanying herself, stating she's "not great at it" and "don't know what to do with my hands," feeling more connected to her performance when playing and singing simultaneously. When recording, she gets a better vocal when singing and playing live together, as overdubbing tends to lead to overthinking and overplaying. "I don't know if people understand what a great pianist you are. I hear it in the, your voicings are incredibly sophisticated."

podcast.title: Post-Grammy Fame Shock
podcast.body: After winning multiple Grammys, Norah Jones experienced an overwhelming and disorienting surge in fame. Her picture appeared on the cover of the New York Post next to Saddam Hussein's with the headline "hunt and destroy," and a subsequent article in the Daily News and New York Post detailed her apartment and rent, leading her to feel unable to return home. "So and the next day my picture was on the cover of the New York Post, Nexus Saddam Hussein's picture. It said hunt and destroy and then it was like a split screen, you know, it was like me and Saddam."

podcast.title: Resilience and Boundaries
podcast.body: Following the intense fame of her first album, Norah Jones learned to establish strong boundaries, becoming "stubborn" and comfortable with saying "no" to demands she felt were not artistically driven, such as a label-requested remix for pop radio. She attributes some of this strength to her mother, a "strong woman." "I think I was very stubborn, so I definitely got comfortable with saying no."

podcast.title: Songwriting Process and Memory
podcast.body: When writing "Come Away With Me" in high school, Norah Jones, a "theory nerd," wrote the song's chords and lyrics in a notebook as she didn't have recording devices. However, she believes the version she later recalled and perfected was "a little different" from her original creation, a detail lost because she couldn't record it. "I think it's a little different. It was a little different than what I had originally come up with and I will never know. Because you didn't remember that. Because I didn't record it."

podcast.title: Wayne Shorter Recording Experience
podcast.body: Norah Jones was extremely nervous and felt "a little under prepared" for her two-day recording session with Wayne Shorter. Despite her apprehension, the experience, including a previous afternoon spent at Wayne's house discussing his comic books and anger-fueled saxophone playing, was "one of the cooler things" she has done. "I was so nervous for it and a little under prepared. I didn't have that many songs."
